papers.abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.
bullets: Introduces an annotated egocentric tennis dataset synchronized with five allocentric views, global positions, contact times, and stroke labels.
Evaluates seven tasks, including player/ball localization, trajectory forecasting, stroke anticipation, contact-time prediction, and contact-position estimation.
Best models reach 0.14 m ego-player and 0.54 m ball localization error, 0.34 m and 0.91 m forecasting error over 1.1 s, and 0.14 s contact-time error.
Auxiliary depth improves 3D ball localization; longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, suggesting reliance on scene context over motion alone.
A conditional diffusion model generates adaptive whole-body tennis motion from vision predictions at real-time rates.

papers.abstract: As egocentric video becomes increasingly available for embodied learning, an important research question is how to turn this low-cost, scalable source of data into robot manipulation capabilities. Egocentric videos naturally provide rich context for high-level task understanding, while real-robot demonstrations with wrist observations and action annotations provide supervision for fine-grained action alignment. We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns object relations, task state, and temporal progress through future prediction on egocentric video. The Interaction module interprets wrist observations in global context and learns local alignment and contact cues through robot action supervision. Separate residual paths expose both representations to the action policy, preserving direct access to task context alongside fine-grained execution information. Ego-CEVR supports independent pretraining of its global video module on large-scale human egocentric videos and videos from diverse robot embodiments, without requiring robot action labels or paired wrist observations.

papers.abstract: Enabling a humanoid to interact naturally with human partners requires preserving not only individual motions but also the spatial, semantic, and contact relationships underlying the interaction (i.e., hugging, dancing, hand-shaking, etc.). Furthermore, a practical solution should generalize across various humanoid embodiments with distinct morphologies and kinematic constraints. To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically plausible human-humanoid interactions. HumiTransfer first reconstructs 3D human motion with consistent foot-ground contact, then transfers one participant to a target humanoid embodiment via interaction modeling, using weighted joint-relative directions and anatomical offsets to prioritize interaction-critical inter-body relationships, while post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings.
authors: Nghia Le (Hann), Khang Nguyen (Hann), Ba Long Tran (Hann), Thi Quynh Nhu Pham (Hann), Binh Nguyen (Hann), Tuong Do (Hann), Erman Tjiputra (Hann), Hoan Nguyen (Hann), Tung D. Ta (Hann), Baoru Huang (Hann), Hai-Nguyen (Hann), Nguyen (Hann), Anh Nguyen

papers.abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand--contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on $43$--$78\%$ of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on $<10\%$ and $22.5\%$ of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12\% to 32\% on GRAB dataset. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
authors: Cunxi Dai, Botao He, Francois R Hogan, Wei Pan, Rao Fu, Wen-Han Hsieh, Ruoshi Liu, Jitendra Malik, Guanya Shi, Akash Sharma
bullets: Addresses the failure of kinematics-only retargeting to preserve the contact dynamics needed for successful manipulation.
Uses a shared hand–contact representation for video, motion capture, and tactile-glove data, generating both robot actions and contact-force targets.
Introduces Vid-HACO for inferring contacts from video and a tactile tracking controller for hardware open-loop replay.
Maintains contact on 43–78% of contact frames, compared with under 10% for kinematic and 22.5% for object-aware retargeting.
Improves strict task success on GRAB from 12% to 32% when integrated with physics-based retargeting; hardware results show tactile tracking is essential for reproducing forces.

papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.

Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.
authors: Qingyuan Cai, Bo Zhang, Yongzhen Huang, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of robot data and the human–robot embodiment gap.
Learns factorized latent actions that disentangle shared manipulation primitives from embodiment-specific signals.
Transfers manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations to robots with different kinematic structures.
Supports both parallel grippers and dexterous hands.
Reports consistent gains over no-pretraining baselines on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors. Yet, existing reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines are limited in system-level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback. We present ViT-H, a video-to-humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm. ViT-H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion-tracking outcomes to post-train the generator with direct preference optimization. We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability. We further show that ViT-H scales favorably with model size and with both pre-training and post-training data scale, while motion-tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers.
bullets: Addresses scalability limits of separately optimized reconstruction–retargeting–tracking pipelines.
Uses a diffusion model to generate humanoid reference motions directly from video, avoiding explicit reconstruction and retargeting.
Applies direct preference optimization based on motion-tracking outcomes to improve executability.
An autoregressive variant supports real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency.
Experiments on the Unitree G1 show improved motion quality and executability, with favorable scaling across model and data size.

papers.abstract: The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. As a result, the same motion can appear at widely different speeds across demonstrations, and policies trained on such data may inherit operator-specific timing along with task behavior. We propose to learn a speed prior directly from large-scale demonstration data. Given a task instruction, a motion path and the images along it, it predicts a distribution over execution speed along the path, from which a chosen quantile defines a consistent clock for retiming each demonstration. Existing methods derive the acceleration signal from the very data they accelerate, so each new task costs another fit, annotation, or pair of predefined rates. A single trained speed prior instead covers every task in a corpus. We fit a speed prior on both robot teleoperation data and handheld demonstrations in which a human arm, rather than a robot arm, moves the gripper, and use it to retime robot demonstrations to the handheld pace before fine-tuning a vision-language-action policy. For execution, we pair the policy with a real-time optimal-control layer that tracks predicted action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace. On 120 RoboLab tasks, policies fine-tuned on our learned clocks succeed more often and move with up to half the jerk compared with policies fine-tuned on the original demonstration timing and uniformly accelerated to the same speed. On a real robot, our policy stacks cups in 3.50s, 1.72$\times$ faster than the default policy's 6.02s while succeeding as often, in 29 of 30 trials. Videos and further material are available at https://mllab.snu.ac.kr/projects/learned_speed_prior.
authors: Seungyong Moon, Deokjae Lee, Hansang Lee, Munkhtselmeg Battsengel, Youngin Kim, Seonghyeon Yun, Sungjin Jeon, SongEun Kim, Jeongmin Park, Hyun Oh Song
bullets: Teleoperator timing can vary across demonstrations and cause policies to learn operator-specific speeds rather than task-relevant motion.
The method predicts a distribution of execution speeds from the task instruction, motion path, and path images; a selected quantile defines each demonstration’s new clock.
One speed prior trained on robot and handheld demonstrations can retime demonstrations across tasks without fitting a separate acceleration model per task.
A real-time optimal-control layer tracks policy action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace.
Across 120 RoboLab tasks, learned retiming improved success and reduced jerk by up to half; a real robot stacked cups in 3.50s with 29/30 successes.

(3) SPLICE joins the running plan to this path at the earliest point it reaches on time. (4) SMOOTH solves one minimum-jerk program through the boxes at their scheduled times, within all limits, giving the new plan.

papers.abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.
authors: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma, Yue Su, Cai Zhou, Xiuwei Xu, Tianle Zhang, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of robot demonstrations and noisy action labels from egocentric videos.
Jointly learns visual future prediction and action generation in a vision-language-action framework.
Uses reliability-conditioned corruption and weighted regression to reduce the impact of unreliable action supervision.
Distills action-relevant structure from clean future observations into representations trained with corrupted futures.
Shows steeper scaling than a baseline, with 20.5% lower real-world open-loop action MSE and an 8.1-point RoboCasa few-shot success improvement at 30,000 pretraining hours.

papers.abstract: How do children learn the meanings of the simple, concrete words that form a majority of their early vocabulary? Statistical information about many word meanings can be recovered from the gradual accumulation of information about the co-occurrence of words with their referents, a proposal known as ``cross-situational learning''. Contrastive vision--language models allow this learning strategy to be tested on egocentric video data capturing children's early real-life experiences with visual and linguistic inputs. Initial successes of this method on small datasets provide a proof-of-concept, but vision models struggle to learn robust visual representations when trained on these same egocentric videos. How dependent is cross-situational word learning performance on the quality of the model's visual representations? And can cross-situational models scale to larger and more diverse datasets? To address these questions, we trained models on the BabyView corpus, including 2,441 hours of longitudinal egocentric video from 48 children. Models trained on this dataset learned object--label mappings, but performance was far higher when they used internet-pretrained visual representations as opposed to when visual representations were learned solely from the developmental video data. Further, the majority of the learning signal was carried by a small proportion of utterances that described a visible referent. Models learned lexical representations that showed recognizable human-like semantic structure, but model performance showed substantially different trajectories over training experiences than those observed in children. Cross-situational learning is a viable word learning strategy for early noun vocabulary, but constructing developmentally plausible models will require understanding how to learn high-quality visual representations from naturalistic data.
authors: Michael C. Frank, Alvin W. M. Tan, Khai Loong Aw, Robert Z. Sparks, Victor Moreno, Grace Keene-Lee, Meesha R. Ryan, Tarun Sepuri, Jane Yang, Virginia A. Marchman, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Bria Long
bullets: Models trained on 2,441 hours of egocentric video from 48 children learned object–label mappings.

Most learning came from utterances describing a currently visible referent.
The learned lexical representations developed recognizable human-like semantic structure.
Model learning trajectories differed substantially from those observed in children.

papers.title: Scaling cross-situational word learning on children's naturalistic experiences
papers.tldr: Cross-situational learning can recover early word meanings from large-scale child-centered video, but it depends strongly on high-quality visual representations and does not yet match children’s learning trajectories.

papers.abstract: Segmenting robot demonstration data into disjoint temporal and semantic subsegments is valuable for learning, cleaning, retrieval, and analysis. Segmentation is often performed manually in a tedious and error prone process. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have the potential for automating this process, but directly ingesting raw multi camera video streams into MLLMs can be costly and can quickly exhaust context windows. In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a novel framework that focuses on the companion stream of robot kinematic data. Inspired by the principle of classical entropy coding, such as Huffman coding, where frequently occurring symbols are represented more compactly, we propose Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs), a discrete kinematic vocabulary designed to compactly represent recurring, temporally localized motion patterns, which we refer to as kinematic events. SMTs are learned by encoding kinematic trajectories with temporal segment supervision and quantizing the resulting features. We use increasingly available robot demonstration subtask annotations to supervise an open language model to interpret the resulting token sequences. Evaluation against human labeled segmentation shows that KiRoSe can substantially outperform baseline segmentation methods in F1 quality and transfers zero shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion, while preserving the language models open vocabulary knowledge. Beyond segmentation, KiRoSe tracks task progress on an unseen robot and detects when an action is being reversed.(website: https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/kirose/)
authors: Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Richard Cheng, Sergey Zakharov, Ken Goldberg
bullets: Targets costly, error-prone manual segmentation of robot demonstrations and avoids feeding raw multiview video into language models.
Learns Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs) to compactly encode recurring, temporally localized kinematic patterns.
Uses subtask annotations to supervise an open language model over SMT sequences.
Outperforms baseline segmentation methods in F1 against human labels and transfers zero-shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion.
Also supports task-progress tracking on an unseen robot and detection of action reversal.

figures.caption: Figure 2: KiRoSe Pipeline. Given a robot kinematic stream and the task instruction “fold the paper box,” KiRoSe encodes motion using a transition-supervised encoder, then temporally pools and quantizes its features into Sparse Motion Tokens with a learned codebook. The language model reads these tokens, time markers, and the instruction to output action descriptions with start and end times, such as “pick up the object,” “place in the box,” and “adjust.” Transition annotations provide training supervision, while the motion tokenizer remains frozen during language-model adaptation.

Figure 5: Qualitative reversal probe on AgiBot (zero-shot). One subtask per episode is played backwards in place (red frames; stamps give original recording time). Curves show the signed progress rate (green: rising, red: falling); dashed: same model on the original video. ReWiND keeps counting up while the task is undone; KiRoSe’s progress falls; Table 4 reports statistic result.

Figure 7: Segmentation examples on held-out YAM tasks (ABC-130K). The zero-shot video model tends to emit a few coarse segments that restate the instruction (“fold and stack blue towel”, “attempt insert plug”), whereas KiRoSe recovers the repeated grasp–place, flatten–fold, and insert cycles of the reference from kinematics alone. KiRoSe’s Boundary F1 at ±1 s exceeds the video baseline on all five episodes (0.44–0.72 versus 0.07–0.38).

papers.abstract: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.

papers.abstract: Long egocentric videos pose a central challenge for multimodal language models: the visual stream must be compressed into a memory representation that can be searched efficiently while still preserving the evidence needed for question answering. Building on an online textual-memory framework in which first-person videos are converted into temporally grounded captions, this work systematically studies the role of retrieval in episodic-memory video question answering. We evaluate how different retrieval units, query formulations, context budgets, and reranking strategies affect multiple-choice answering on QAEgo4D-Closed, isolating retrieval as the main variable while keeping the underlying generated memory fixed. Our best configuration, Parent, matches fine-grained caption subchunks, then provides their full parent captions to the reasoner. It achieves 56.4 % accuracy, matching strong full-memory and retrieval baselines while exposing only a small fraction of the textual memory at question time. More importantly, our analysis shows that better temporal coverage does not necessarily translate into better answers: increasing the retrieval budget improves temporal Hit@K and Recall@K, but can reduce accuracy by introducing visually plausible distractors and uncertain caption evidence. These findings suggest that retrieval-augmented egocentric memory should not be optimized only for evidence recall, but also for the reliability, specificity, and answer-discriminative value of the retrieved context. The study motivates more structured episodic memories that move beyond raw caption retrieval toward evidence-aware representations for long-form egocentric reasoning.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion-tracking policies can reproduce diverse behaviors, yet connecting independently acquired motions into a continuous sequence remains challenging. Interpolation connects boundary poses without considering whether their relative position, heading, and timing provide suitable conditions for a transition. A generative motion prior can produce richer motion, but poorly arranged boundaries may cause it to generate excessive locomotion, turning, or another unintended action. We present Spatio-Temporal Alignment with a Motion Prior (STAMP), a framework for connecting independently acquired humanoid motions through a Robot-to-Human-to-Robot process. STAMP uses human motion space to draw on rich motion priors and reuse transition knowledge across robot embodiments. Its key component is a learned alignment model that determines the boundary conditions for motion inbetweening. Given the two motions retargeted to a human rig, the alignment model ranks candidate positions, headings, and transition durations for the following motion. A human motion prior generates the transition under the selected alignment. The completed sequence is retargeted to the robot and used as a reference to train a motion-tracking policy. We evaluate the tracking success of the generated transitions on Unitree~G1 and~ROBOTIS K1. Physical robot demonstrations further show that STAMP connects independently acquired motions into long-horizon sequences. Project page: https://childtoy.github.io/STAMP-project

papers.abstract: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.
authors: Xiongbo Shi, Shihang Du, Zongyou Yu, Ao Zhou, Xudong Zhang, Ziyu Lin, Haodong Zhang, Junqiao Zhao, Guang Chen

Adds Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring to refine object-surface contacts, and STRL uses adaptive key-stage sampling with contact-aware rewards.

Both enter the constrained optimization to produce dense robot references. papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without finetuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Recovering metric world-space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi-stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out-of-view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world-space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi-stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single-stage pipeline. To resolve metric-scale ambiguity, it combines scene-level geometric features from VGGT-$\Omega$ with metric-space supervision, while hand-specific features preserve fine-grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out-of-view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world-space accuracy and temporal consistency over state-of-the-art methods. DewHand reduces rigid-aligned world-space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero-shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid-aligned world-space error (WA-MPJPE) on each dataset.

bullets: Addresses error propagation, monocular scale ambiguity, and ambiguous motion from occlusion or out-of-view hands.

papers.abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine's tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/.
authors: Matthew Strong, Ankush K. Dhawan, Julien Poffet, Giuse Pham, Jinho So, Monroe Kennedy III
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable robot-learning data without depth sensors, robot hardware, or restricting augmentation to demonstrated objects.
Tracks object 3D poses using DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats and aligns photograph-based digital object “cousins” to demonstrated objects and functional regions.
Maps the human hand motion to feasible robot grasps and generates demonstrations in IsaacSim or MuJoCo.
Generates over 2,000 episodes in about two hours and supports training from one human video per task.
Across two real robots and four tasks, policies trained on generated data match or exceed teleoperation-trained policies across diverse object instances.

papers.abstract: Active perception is essential for robotic manipulation when fixed viewpoints leave task-relevant information occluded or unobserved. However, enabling vision-language-action (VLA) models to reason across changing viewpoints and actively acquire informative observations remains challenging. We present ActiveScale, a framework that advances active perception through coordinated model, data, and hardware designs. Our model augments a VLA with historical video observations and explicit camera-pose supervision, using per-frame pose tokens and a lightweight prediction head to associate observations across viewpoints and support a coherent understanding of the scene. To learn from the camera motion naturally present in human activity, we introduce a scalable human--robot mid-training recipe using 1000 hours of egocentric and robotic data, adapting the model to temporal inputs and pose supervision. We further introduce Active-perception Mobile-manipulation Platform (AMP), a robotic platform that supports active perception and mobile manipulation through single-operator teleoperation, enabling scalable collection of demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes and manipulation. Experiments demonstrate improved success rates on active-perception tasks, while ablation studies validate the contributions of camera-pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training. Together, these components provide an integrated foundation for studying and developing active perception in robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses occlusion and missing task information caused by fixed viewpoints in robotic manipulation.
Augments a vision-language-action model with historical video, per-frame camera-pose tokens, and pose supervision.
Uses 1000 hours of egocentric and robotic data for human–robot mid-training on temporal inputs and camera motion.
Introduces AMP, a teleoperable platform for collecting demonstrations that coordinate viewpoint changes with manipulation.
Experiments report improved active-perception success rates; ablations support pose-aware modeling and egocentric mid-training.

Pose-grounded camera tokens support camera-pose reconstruction, while the VLM predicts semantic outputs such as subtasks and a flow-matching action expert generates manipulation and active-camera actions. The architecture is shared across human and robot training data.
Fig. 2: AMP system overview. Left: Single-operator Meta Quest 2 interface. Right: AMP triple-arm robotic platform.

Fig. 4: Overview of the five real-world active-perception task families, grouped into two complementary settings: Occlusion-Driven Manipulation (Bag, Drawer, and Table), where task-relevant objects are initially hidden or outside the default view, and Active Search and Localization (Pot and Box), where the robot must actively search across workspace regions and localize instructed objects or targets.

papers.abstract: Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion. Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene. For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene. Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video-motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion. Videos and additional results are available on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/par/projects/jca/.
authors: Noam Rotstein, Yoad Tewel, Chen Tessler, Haggai Maron, Gal Chechik, Or Litany, Yoni Kasten, Yuval Atzmon
bullets: Addresses the gap between realistic video generation and usable 3D animation for specific assets.
Separates an arbitrary-skeleton 3D motion model from a pretrained video model, linking them with lightweight cross-attention.
Predicts joint locations in video to recover the camera and register 3D motion in the scene.
Uses curated synthetic edits plus human and robot video to create nearly 200K training pairs.
Supports text-to-motion/video, video-to-rig motion, rig-motion-to-video, and keyframe control; evaluations report more faithful, scene-responsive animation than video-first pipelines.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview. Given a text prompt, a rig, and an optional reference image, the model jointly denoises video latents Zv and motion tokens Zm. A graph network encodes the rig into per-joint descriptors D, using the joints’ 2D locations in the reference image, and these condition the motion branch; a graph-attention layer inside each Motion DiT block propagates features along the rig edges. Zero-initialized cross-attention bridges exchange features in both directions at paired blocks, each branch querying the other’s intermediate features, so joint training begins from the two pretrained branches acting as they did in isolation. An auxiliary joint-localization head (right) attends from joint features to video patches and returns each joint’s image position as a weighted combination of patch coordinates, giving 2D–3D correspondences used to fit a camera.

Figure 3: Text-driven rig animation across diverse assets. Each row shows a text prompt, an input mesh, and sampled poses from animations generated by competing methods and JCA (ours). Our method more faithfully captures the requested actions while preserving the asset’s geometry.

Figure 5: Scene-aware rig animation and motion localization. Given a penguin rig, a rendered initial frame of a snowy 3D scene, and a text prompt, our model jointly generates video and 3D rig motion. Top: frames from the generated video, where the penguin moves forward and slides down the snowy slope. Middle: the raw 3D motion produced by the motion branch, rendered in the input scene before localization. The penguin’s motion is not aligned with the depicted scene geometry and, in later frames, appears beneath the snow surface. Bottom: the same generated motion after applying our joint-localization and camera-alignment scheme described in section 3.3. The estimated alignment correctly places the motion on the visible penguin and registers it with the generated video and scene.

Figure 6: Prompt-adherence evaluation of one animation with GPT-6 Astra. In the first turn, the judge is given the asset’s short description and 48 frames of the animation, 16 from each of the front, right, and left views, each frame labeled with its view; the figure shows two frames per view. It is asked to describe the motion it observes in chronological order. In the second turn, it scores the motion against the action prompt. The complete prompts and responses are given in section B.3.

papers.abstract: Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex, a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds---from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video---into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world. Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex/.
authors: Yuxuan Kuang, Jiashun Wang, Yixuan Sun, Yufei Ye, Sungjae Park, Umar Iqbal, Katerina Fragkiadaki, Shubham Tulsiani
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between natural human-like behavior and robustness to varied object poses and goals.
Uses Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking: a shared policy learns from dense motion tracking and sparse object-success objectives in parallel environments.
Supports demonstrations from mocap or hand–object reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video.
Learns skills including functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and throw-and-catch.
Reports improved generalization and functionality over baselines, with transfer across simulators and to the real world.

figures.caption: Figure 7: Overview of our RGB-D hand-object reconstruction pipeline. Given an RGB-D video and camera intrinsics, we recover hand motion with Dyn-HaMR, reconstruct a metric object mesh with SAM 3D, and track its pose with FoundationPose++. A table plane is estimated from depth points using RANSAC. We align hand translations to the observed depth, then apply GeoCalibbased gravity alignment and table-height alignment to express the hand, object, and table in a shared world coordinate frame.

Figure 5: ADADEX learns diverse skills such as functional grasping, in-hand reorientation, dynamic throw-and-catch, and can achieve various downstream tasks with high dexterity. Our method also works on various robot hand embodiments and real arm-hand systems.

Figure 2: Left: Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking is a goal-conditioned RL formulation in which dense reference tracking and sparse goal reaching are trained as parallel environment types under a single shared actor. Right: our method can learn adaptable dexterous skills with a single human motion reconstructed from video and transfer to an unseen simulator (MuJoCo) and the real world.
Figure 3: Qualitative comparisons. Trained on a single human motion, ADADEX can track seen and unseen motions naturally, while baselines struggle with generalization and functionality.
Figure 4: Setting (iv): comparison on tracking real-to-sim HOI motions.
Figure 6: Sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer, in real time (1x speed, 30 Hz), demonstrating physical feasibility of the learned dexterous behaviors.
Table 1: Motion tracking performance on (i) seen motions and (ii) similar but unseen motions. Best and second-best mean values for each metric within each setting are bolded and underlined.
Table 4: Network details and training hyperparameters.
Table 2: Setting (iii): random goal reaching comparison over the 12 GRAB objects.

Table 6: Benchmark motions: 12 distinct GRAB objects with one seconds-long motion each, 24 unseen GRAB motions (2 for each object), and 9 real-to-sim motions. Frames refer to the frame length of the trimmed motions for training; for unseen GRAB motions, they refer to the evaluated reference movement windows. All motions are in 60 Hz.

papers.abstract: Humanoid-human interaction requires robots to operate under severe partial observability: during close physical contact, the human partner is occluded, truncated, or outside the robot's field of view, causing pose estimation to fail and often necessitating external tracking or privileged human state. At the same time, heavy mutual occlusions introduce errors into the human-human motion-capture data used for learning. We present REACT, a framework for learning deployable humanoid-human interaction policies from human-human demonstrations. REACT treats semantic contact structure as the key supervisory signal connecting demonstration processing, interaction learning, and onboard control. First, a VLM-guided contact modeling and retargeting pipeline identifies semantically meaningful contacts and transfers them onto humanoid-human geometry while preserving interaction structure. Using these annotations, privileged interaction policies learn physically grounded behaviors through interaction-aware contact rewards and are then distilled into deployable egocentric depth policies trained entirely from onboard sensing using photorealistic human depth rendering. To address severe partial observability, we introduce generative partner-state modeling objectives that predict partner motion from occluded egocentric views. We evaluate REACT in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid across five contact-rich interactions. Semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interactions, while generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most under heavy occlusion. On real hardware, REACT performs all five interactions using onboard sensing alone.
authors: Yuto Shibata, Kotaro Amaya, Kashu Yamazaki, Lalit Jayanti, Yoshimitsu Aoki, Mariko Isogawa, Katerina Fragkiadaki
bullets: Addresses partial observability and occlusion that make human pose estimation unreliable during close contact.
Uses semantic contact annotations to retarget human-human demonstrations onto humanoid-human geometry while preserving interaction structure.
Learns privileged interaction policies with contact-aware rewards, then distills them into egocentric depth policies using onboard sensing.
Generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall in four of five evaluated interactions, especially under heavy occlusion.
Demonstrated all five contact-rich interactions in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 using onboard sensing alone.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of REACT. REACT first annotates semantic contacts in human–human demonstrations with a VLM and retargets them onto the humanoid while preserving them. A privileged teacher then learns the interaction with contact rewards and is finally distilled into an egocentric depth student that predicts the partner’s motion and runs on the real robot.
Figure 4: Student rollouts on held-out motions in simulation (inset: egocentric depth input)

Figure 6: Long-horizon behavior: three consecutive hugs in a single episode. A continuous ∼30 s rollout in which the policy completes the hug interaction three times in a row, with no reset or re-initialisation between repetitions. The ten snapshots are read in boustrophedon order, following the arrows. After each embrace the robot releases the partner, re-approaches, and re-establishes contact, so the three hug cycles appear as three separate close-contact phases across the panels. The policy sustains repeated contact-rich interaction over a long horizon rather than a single one-shot contact.

Figure 7: VLM skill-selection state machine. Solid boxes are states and dashed boxes are the policies they invoke: the HOMIE locomotion controller for Search, Approach, and Retreat, and one of the five per-interaction students for Interact.

Figure 3: Within each interaction, frames are split into moments when the partner is hard to see (blue), either too close to fit in the view or largely out of view, and the remaining frames (gray). (Appendix C.4).

Figure 13: Qualitative retargeting comparison. Rows: the five contact-rich actions (hug, handshake, pat-on-back, high-five, link-arms). Columns: the original human–human demonstration and four retargets (GMR, OmniRetarget, Ours w/o VLM filtering, Ours), each at the action’s peak-contact frame. The red arrow marks the demonstrated contact the retarget must reproduce on the G1. Ours establishes the touch on the robot surface where the baselines reach short or push apart.

Figure 10: Why the external pose estimation-based method fails at contact range. Temporally ordered snapshots of an external-pose rollout, read left to right, with the ground-truth partner (green, Human (Sim)) and the HMR2.0 reconstruction (red, HMR2.0 Prediction) overlaid against the robot (black). Left three: high-five; as the partner’s hand leaves the robot’s egocentric field of view, the reconstructed hand position deviates sharply from the ground truth at the moment of contact. Right three: hug; at the instant of embrace the partner’s torso occludes the camera, and the reconstruction collapses into a large error behind the true mesh. The estimator degrades precisely in the close-contact, self-occluded regime that REACT’s end-to-end student handles directly from depth.

Figure 12: Body correspondence projects the SMPL-X mesh onto either the G1 or the partnercapsule surface. The offline registration introduced in Sec. D.2 establishes a dense body correspondence that maps every SMPL-X body vertex to a (link, plocal) pair, so the same mesh can be projected onto either target surface, the Unitree G1 robot or the partner’s SMPL-X collision capsules. The three columns show one identical set of colour-coded SMPL-X vertices in three configurations, from left to right: projected onto the G1 robot surface, in their SMPL-X template positions, and projected onto the partner capsule surface. Each colour denotes the G1 link a vertex is registered to, and the connecting lines join the same representative vertices across the three configurations, so that any contact vertex can be carried onto the corresponding robot or capsule surface by forward kinematics. The columns are drawn at true relative scale, exposing the proportion mismatch between the human template and the shorter G1 that the registration must bridge. The dense map covers the full template at a mean vertex-to-surface residual of 0.89mm, well below the ϵ = 10 cm contact threshold.

Figure 11: VLM contact filtering, qualitative examples. Distance candidates and their VLM verdicts on the five contact-rich Inter-X actions (rows: hug, hand-shake, pat-on-back, high-five, link-arms), sampled at 1 s intervals over a 4 s window (columns). Green markers are candidates kept after VLM verification, labelled essential or incidental. Red markers are Stage 1 distance candidates the VLM removes as spurious near-contacts. The proximity test fires on many transient arm passes; the VLM stage prunes them while preserving the genuine contacts, which is the precision gain quantified in Tab. 8.

Figure 14: User-study web interface (one trial). The original demonstration (3-view orbit, top) and the four blinded retarget conditions A–D (middle) are played synchronously; the participant gives a strict 1–4 ranking for each of the three questions (bottom). Full ranking criteria are in Sec. E.5.

Figure 5: Generalization across partner distance and orientation. REACT performs pat-on-back with the partner at 70 cm and 130 cm and with the partner back-on or side-on to the robot; the per-interaction student reaches and holds the back contact in every condition from onboard depth alone.

Figure 8: One continuous rollout with VLM skill selection. No interaction is specified in advance. From left to right: the partner opens their arms, and the VLM selects the hug student; the partner is then displaced mid-rollout, and the robot re-finds them, approaches, and switches to the hand-shake student, all without a reset.

Figure 9: In-loop human depth rendering closes the sim-to-real gap. Egocentric depth of a hug frame. Capsule: the partner as collision primitives, blocky and non-human. SMPL-X Mesh: the partner rendered as a realistic body mesh. SMPL-X Mesh + Scene (Ours): our full rendering with the randomised scene. This last variant closely resembles the real-sensor depth shown in Figure 1 of the main paper.

Ext. human pose (HMR2.0) drives the policy from partner state produced by an external human-pose estimator while Ours (E2E) outputs actions end-to-end from egocentric depth and proprioception. Both rows use earlier model settings than Table 3 and are evaluated on the same held-out motions.

Table 7: Teacher vs. student contact recall (%) on matched motions. T: privileged teacher, S: egocentric depth student, Rec.: S/T. The mean recovery averages the per-interaction ratios.

papers.title: VLM-Guided Contact Retargeting and Generative Partner Modeling for Humanoid-Human Interaction
papers.tldr: REACT enables a humanoid to perform contact-rich human interactions from onboard sensing by combining VLM-guided contact retargeting, policy distillation, and generative partner-state prediction.

papers.abstract: Understanding contact and tactile magnitude in hand-object interaction is a key step toward physically intelligent systems, yet learning such representations is limited by the cost and restricted coverage of tactile measurements. We present Touch-JEPA, a framework for learning tactile representations from hand-object videos with limited tactile supervision. We first introduce a self-supervised pretraining objective that learns from video alone without tactile supervision. Using video-derived hand geometry, Touch-JEPA predicts masked visual features at corresponding hand-surface locations from spatial and temporal context, encouraging the representation to capture latent contact dynamics. We then extend this formulation to joint representation learning, where masked prediction is applied to all videos while tactile supervision is available only for a labeled subset, grounding the shared representation in measured contact and magnitude. With self-supervised pretraining alone, simple supervised readouts on frozen Touch-JEPA features outperform supervised baselines in contact discrimination and tactile magnitude estimation across three human-hand benchmarks, and transfer to robotic hands without robot tactile training data. Joint learning with limited tactile supervision further improves contact and magnitude estimation on the human-hand benchmarks. Together, these results show that hand-object video can provide scalable self-supervision for tactile representation learning, while limited tactile measurements provide complementary physical grounding.

papers.abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.
authors: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Existing condition-guided methods suffer from geometric estimation errors, while motion-only transfer often loses contact dynamics and causes hand collapse.

EgoActionBench evaluates action preservation, visual quality, and hand–object plausibility; experiments report more coherent and physically plausible videos than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed framework. Given an egocentric manipulation video, our framework uses a reference branch and an optimized generation branch for test-time action transfer. We apply Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring (VSA) in the early denoising steps to preserve hand-object structure, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration (SCC) in the mid-to-late steps to refine local correspondences and improve interaction realism.

Figure 6. The overview of EgoActionBench. EgoActionBench contains 350 reference manipulation videos and 1,400 target prompts, covering indoor/outdoor scenes, single-/two-hand interactions, and diverse manipulation categories. The benchmark evaluates whether generated videos preserve the reference action semantics while adapting to new visual contexts.

Figure 5. Gallery of proposed method. EgoACT can transfer a wide range of egocentric manipulation videos, covering diverse interaction categories, object types, and motion patterns. The generated videos preserve plausible hand-object structure, contact dynamics, and temporal coherence while adapting the reference action to new visual contexts.

Figure 16. More Comparison with Baseline. Our method consistently produces more coherent action transfer and more plausible handobject interactions than baselines, which often suffer from structural collapse, temporal inconsistency, or physically unrealistic interactions.

Figure 14. Failure case. Our method may struggle with actions involving very fast hand or object motion, which can lead to motion blur, temporal aliasing, or loss of hand-object correspondence. This limitation is primarily due to the base video diffusion model, which was not specifically trained to handle rapid egocentric dynamics and tends to produce temporally smoothed outputs when the inter-frame displacement is large.
Figure 8. Qualitative comparison. Compare with previous methods, our method preserves stable hand-object layout and object response.

Figure 4. Illustration of the proposed SCC. (a) Direct transfer injects the reference action without correction, which may lead to errors in weak hand-object interactions. (b) Applying correction throughout the whole denoising process over-constrains early generation, making it difficult to decouple transferable action from source observation. (c) Our SCC performs sparse correspondence calibration only in the mid-to-late denoising stages, where the action layout has been established and local interaction details can be refined, improving temporal consistency and hand-object realism.

papers.abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. papers.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/
authors: Oliver Hausd\"orfer, Felix Minzenmay, Mani Majd, Maximilian P. Christof, Shiyuan Zhang, Angela P. Schoellig
bullets: Single-view latent action models ambiguously infer 6D movements, especially out-of-plane actions and occluded interactions.

Dual-view pretraining improves 6D-action decodability by 17% over single-view and yields a +13.5% downstream success-rate gain versus +6.2% for single-view.
One cross-embodiment source is sufficient for skill transfer; adding a second viewpoint is more beneficial than adding up to four additional embodiments.
Hardware experiments using human-hand demonstrations improve success by 20% over action-only policies across 850 rollouts, with benefits varying by task.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Method: We combine latent action pretraining from in-domain cross-embodiment videos with a downstream flow-matching policy. First, latent actions are inferred from a large cross-embodiment video dataset. Second, a sequential policy is learned on the latent actions and a small set of demonstrations on the target embodiment. The LAM uses a spatio-temporal transformer to merge multiple viewpoints before computing the latents. The spatial block attends to patches of other viewpoints, yielding latent actions grounded in 3D space. Latent action labels and real robot actions are jointly used to train a hierarchical downstream policy. The policy uses sequential flow matching experts and outputs actions applied to the robot.
Fig. 8. Failure modes. Models struggle with object grasping (44% of failure cases). The push task requires precision to align the gripper with the milk.

The multi-view LAM shows significantly better reconstruction of the ground-truth robot motion in y-direction. See more qualitative results in the supplementary video.

papers.abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0, the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data, comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop, a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, $\Psi_0$, $\omega$-HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world-action modeling further demonstrate the model's utility for embodied decision-making.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video supports diverse applications, including robot learning, augmented reality, and human activity understanding. Recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from such video requires estimating both hand motion and camera egomotion to express the hands in a consistent reference frame. Many existing pipelines recover hand and camera motion in separate stages, combining hand detection, hand reconstruction, camera tracking, and trajectory refinement. We present V-JEPA Hand, a simple feed-forward video model that jointly reconstructs bilateral hand motion and camera motion from egocentric clips. It uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to extract spatio-temporal features from full-frame video and a query-based predictor to decode these features into per-frame hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion. We use the predicted camera motion to express the hand trajectories in a common world frame. The model accepts known focal lengths or predicts them when unavailable. It reconstructs each clip in a single forward pass. We train both components end to end in a single stage on a mixture of diverse pseudo-labelled videos and high-precision 3D annotations. A single model achieves the lowest coverage-aware mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard. It also yields lower world-frame trajectory errors than the compared SLAM-based pipelines. Ablations support the benefits of video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision. V-JEPA Hand achieves a forward-pass throughput of 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000. Project page: https://qft-333.github.io/V-JEPA-Hand-Page/.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing human activity from egocentric video requires more than recovering individual 3D components: the observer's motion, surrounding geometry, and hand-object interactions must fit together in a consistent world. Achieving this coherence requires both joint reconstruction and aligned supervision, yet existing methods and datasets offer limited support for either. We present EgoXperience, a full-stack paradigm that addresses these needs through data collection, automatic annotation, unified modeling, and benchmarking. Central to EgoXperience is an automatic annotation engine, EgoX-Engine, that couples geometrically verified object tracking with SLAM-based world alignment, yielding consistent supervision for the camera, scene, hands, and objects. This yields EgoX-Data-6M, a 50-hour dataset of task-driven manipulation and locomotion within and across indoor and outdoor environments, with second-level task captions. We carefully select one hour across these activity categories as EgoX-Bench to evaluate joint reconstruction. To translate this supervision into reconstruction, we introduce EgoX, trained with EgoX-Data-6M and complementary annotations from additional public datasets. Given monocular egocentric video and first-frame object masks, our model achieves joint metric reconstruction of the camera, scene, hands, and objects in a shared world coordinate frame with a single forward pass. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across scene estimation and world-space hand-object pose recovery. Against the strongest evaluated baselines, EgoX reduces camera, hand, and depth errors by 68.9%, 65.6%, and 42.9%, and improves object pose scores by 28.0%.

papers.abstract: Human egocentric experience offers a rich foundation for learning how the world is organized and how it changes through interaction. Realizing this potential at scale requires turning growing volumes of recordings into learning resources that connect scene structure, object semantics, and interaction histories across viewpoints and time, while reducing dependence on costly manual annotation. We introduce HOLI-WORLD, an integrated ecosystem connecting experience capture, world representation, automated data construction, model learning, and independent evaluation. To sup- port learning at scale, HOLIWORLD-Foundry combines complementary static and dynamic perception to automatically construct world records that connect persistent scene structure and evolving object states with interaction histories and supporting observations. HOLIWORLD-Data organizes these records from approximately 100 self-collected scenes into grounded learning resources, including approximately 80K QA pairs used to train HOLIWORLD-VL-4B. Independent human annotations of heldout recordings form HOLIWORLD-Bench, supporting evaluation of both annotation quality and learned spatial and temporal understanding. Experiments on ScanNet, ScanNet++, Aria Digital Twin, and HOLIWORLD-Bench demonstrate strong performance in static perception and dynamic tracking, while training on HOLIWORLD-Data substantially improves HOLIWORLD-VL-4B's spatial and temporal reasoning on HOLI- WORLD-Bench and EgoDynamic4D. HOLIWORLD provides a practical foundation for expanding learning resources from the continuous flow of human experience and advancing machine understanding of the dynamic world.

papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstration (LfD) allows robots to learn new skills from human examples; however, many vision-based methods require large datasets and resource-intensive end-to-end training. This paper introduces a data-efficient LfD framework for humanoid robots that learns manipulation skills from compact, task-specific features instead of raw images. The proposed approach integrates layered visual preprocessing, Kinect-based human joint estimation, prompt-based object detection, and depth information to extract human motion features and three-dimensional object locations from demonstration videos. These features are used to train a temporal deep learning model that predicts robot joint-angle trajectories for execution. The framework is implemented on a NAO humanoid robot, evaluated quantitatively in simulation, and demonstrated on physical hardware. In simulation, the robot achieves a 78% success rate on a pick-and-place task using only 16 demonstrations, which increases to 86% when trained with 100 demonstrations. The framework also achieves a 71% success rate on a pushing task using eight demonstrations, highlighting its effectiveness for data-efficient humanoid skill acquisition.
